samples.text:
In some countries, public places like museums, libraries and parks now get a lot of their money from private companies. I think this is a positive development, because without this money many of these places could not survive.

The main reason is that governments often do not have enough money. They have to spend their budget on important things like hospitals, schools and the police, so culture and parks are not a priority. When a company give money, a museum can stay open, buy new exhibitions and keep its entrance free. A library can buy more books and computers, and a park can have new playgrounds and better cleaning.

Another reason is that both sides get benefits. The companies get good advertising, because people see their name and logo in the museum or the park, and they think the company is responsible and care about society. At the same time, the public can enjoy better facilities without paying more tax. So it is a win-win situation.

However, there are some risks. A company may want to control what a museum shows, or it may use the museum to hide bad things it has done, for example an oil company that pollute the environment. Also, if the company decides to stop giving money, the facility can have serious financial problems.

In conclusion, I believe it is a positive development that public facilities get money from private companies, because it helps them to provide better services for people. However, the government should make rules so that companies cannot control the content, and it should still give some money itself.
samples.why: Clear positive position · relevant ideas with simple examples but limited analysis · basic, repetitive linking · adequate vocabulary with some informal choices (win-win) · agreement errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
In many countries, museums, libraries and public parks are relying more and more on sponsorship and donations from private businesses to cover their costs. Although this extra funding brings short-term benefits, I believe that growing dependence on it is a negative development.

It is easy to see why such partnerships are attractive. Public budgets are under pressure, and cultural institutions and green spaces are often among the first areas to face cuts. Corporate money can pay for new exhibitions, longer opening hours or improved facilities, and companies gain a positive public image in return.

However, the first problem is that sponsorship can affect what these institutions do. A museum that depends on a particular company may be reluctant to host an exhibition that criticises that company's industry. Similarly, sponsors naturally prefer popular, eye-catching projects that attract publicity, so less glamorous work, such as preserving archives or running services in poorer neighbourhoods, may be neglected. Over time, decisions that should be made in the public interest become shaped by commercial priorities.

A second concern is instability. Private funding depends on a company's profits and marketing strategy, both of which can change quickly. If a sponsor withdraws during an economic downturn, a library or park that has come to rely on its money may be forced to reduce services suddenly. Moreover, heavy reliance on corporate support can give governments an excuse to reduce their own responsibility for funding facilities that all citizens is entitled to use.

In conclusion, while private contributions can be a useful addition to public funding, facilities that depend on them risk losing their independence and financial security. For these reasons, I regard this trend as mainly negative, and I believe governments should remain the main source of funding.
samples.why: Clear negative position throughout · concession then two well-extended arguments · clear central topic per paragraph · good vocabulary (eye-catching, economic downturn) · frequent error-free sentences with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Faced with tight public budgets, many museums, libraries and parks have turned to corporate sponsors to fund everything from new galleries to playground equipment. Private support can be a welcome supplement, but when these institutions come to depend on it, I believe the development becomes a largely negative one.

The attraction of corporate money is understandable. Governments must balance cultural spending against the more pressing demands of healthcare, education and security, and in lean years it is often facilities such as libraries that suffer most. Sponsorship can keep doors open and admission free, and companies are often happy to fund projects that associate their brand with public benefit.

The difficulty is that funding is rarely neutral. Institutions that depend on a particular sponsor face a quiet but persistent pressure to avoid offending it, whether by declining an exhibition critical of its industry or by giving its logo prominence it has not earned. In some cases, sponsorship has been used by companies with poor environmental or ethical records to acquire respectability, a practice that implicates the institution in their public relations. Even without any direct interference, sponsors' preference for high-profile, marketable projects can divert resources from essential but unglamorous work, such as conservation or outreach to disadvantaged communities.

Dependence also creates fragility. Corporate budgets fluctuate with profits and marketing fashions, and a facility that has built its operations around a single donor can be left in crisis when that support is withdrawn. Perhaps most significantly, the availability of private money allows governments to retreat from funding institutions that exist precisely because they serve everyone, not just those who are commercially valuable.

In conclusion, private contributions have a legitimate role as an addition to public funding, but reliance on them compromises the independence and stability of institutions that belong to the public. The growing dependence described is therefore a trend that should be resisted rather than encouraged.
samples.why: Clear, carefully qualified negative judgement · sophisticated arguments on independence and fragility fully developed · seamless cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (implicates, fragility) · wide range of accurate complex structures.
